PlantGuard looks at a photograph of a single crop leaf and tells you which of 38 conditions across 14 crops it most resembles, along with how much confidence to place in that reading. It then offers general, non-chemical management practice and names the source it came from.
Everything happens on your phone. The app holds no internet permission at all, so your photos cannot be uploaded anywhere, and it works with no signal.

The model was trained mostly on laboratory photographs, taken against plain backgrounds under even light, and it is substantially less accurate on real photographs taken in a field. Measured on %3$d real field photographs it named the right condition about %1$d%% of the time (macro-F1 about %2$d%%). On laboratory images it scores far higher — treat that higher figure as the best case, not what to expect outdoors.

A confident answer names one condition and is right about %1$d%% of the time. A "possible matches" answer shows three candidates because the single best guess is right only about %2$d%% of the time, while the correct answer is among the three about %3$d%% of the time. "Not recognised" usually means the plant is not one of the 38 covered — not that your photo was bad.

38 conditions across 14 crops: apple, blueberry, cherry, corn (maize), grape, orange, peach, bell pepper, potato, raspberry, soybean, squash, strawberry and tomato. Twelve of the 38 are the healthy state of a crop. Anything outside this list cannot be identified, however clear the photo.

This app is a second opinion, never the decision. PlantGuard never recommends a chemical, a dose or a spraying schedule; for anything you intend to act on, confirm with your local KVK (Krishi Vigyan Kendra) or agricultural extension officer.
How to take a good photo
Framing changes the answer more than anything else you control. A well-framed leaf is far more likely to get a confident reading than a distant or cluttered one.
Pick the single most affected leaf and let it fill most of the picture. Several overlapping leaves give the model competing evidence and usually produce a hedged answer.
Come in to about a hand\'s width from the leaf. A photo of a whole plant or a whole row is too far away for the lesions to be visible.
Hold still and let the camera focus before you tap. Steady the leaf with your other hand if there is a breeze.
Open shade or an overcast sky is ideal. Hard midday sun throws strong shadows and shiny highlights across the leaf, both of which hide the very spots that matter.
Holding the leaf against your hand, a sleeve or bare soil separates it from the clutter behind it.
Photograph the leaf flat-on rather than edge-on, and include the affected area near the middle of the frame — the app analyses the centre square of your photo.
PlantGuard is a learning aid, not a diagnosis. It recognises 38 conditions across 14 crops from a photograph of a single leaf, entirely on your phone.

It was trained mostly on laboratory photographs and is substantially less accurate on real photographs taken in a field. It will sometimes be confidently wrong, and it cannot recognise any plant outside those 38 conditions.
Never make a crop-protection decision based on this app alone. Always confirm any diagnosis with your local KVK (Krishi Vigyan Kendra) or agricultural extension officer before taking action.
